findings.quote: a small (125 mL) glass of wine
findings.explanation: A 125 mL glass of 12% wine is 1.5 units (125 x 12 / 1000), about 1.6 at 13%; the NHS units page this entity cites gives 1.5 for exactly this glass. One unit of wine is roughly 76-83 mL. As written, someone counting small glasses would under-count wine by a third, so '14 units' would really be about 21, 50% over the limit stated in the same bullet. The beer (half a pint at about 3.6%) and spirit (25 mL at 40%) equivalents are correct.
findings.suggestedFix: Say a small (125 mL) glass of wine is about 1.5 units, or give the rule (ABV % x mL / 1000), or drop the wine example.

findings.quote: Continuous, low-dose X-ray imaging shown as a live moving picture
findings.explanation: The summary (what cards and search snippets show) calls fluoroscopy low-dose, but the same page rates radiation 'moderate', says dose is 'highly variable and governed by screening time', cites the FDA that fluoroscopy 'can deliver relatively high doses' in complex interventional work, lists barium bowel studies among the higher-dose examinations and warns of skin injury and cataract. A low dose rate is not a low-dose examination.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop 'low-dose' (for example 'Continuous X-ray imaging shown as a live moving picture ...; dose depends on screening time').

findings.quote: trans women are eligible after at least two years of feminising hormones
findings.explanation: As I recall, UK screening guidance for trans women (and the UCSF and Endocrine Society guidance this site cites on the trans health page) ties breast screening to about five years of feminising hormones, not two; I could not open the cited gov.uk page. The two-year figure appears nowhere else in the slice (health/transgender-health says only 'years of feminising hormones'; imaging/mammography says 'long-term oestrogen') and is repeated in guidance[2]. An eligibility threshold that is wrong in either direction misleads readers about whether to ask for screening.
findings.suggestedFix: Check the figure against the cited UK Government screening page and correct both occurrences (body[3] and guidance[2]); if it cannot be confirmed, say 'after several years of feminising hormones'.

findings.quote: ACE inhibitors act one step upstream by preventing angiotensin II from being made at all.
findings.explanation: Contradicts targets/angiotensin-converting-enzyme, which correctly says angiotensin II can still be made by other enzymes (so ACE inhibition lowers rather than abolishes it, and ARBs remain a useful alternative). 'At all' overstates.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'by reducing how much angiotensin II is made (some is still made by other enzymes)'.

findings.quote: the same transporter in the inner ear accounts for their rare ototoxicity at high doses
findings.explanation: NKCC2 (SLC12A1) is expressed in the kidney (thick ascending limb, macula densa). The cochlear target implicated in loop-diuretic ototoxicity is the related NKCC1 (SLC12A2) in the stria vascularis. The page also contradicts itself: its location field says 'a related isoform is in the inner ear'.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'the related NKCC1 transporter in the inner ear (stria vascularis) accounts for ...'.

findings.quote: penicillins
findings.explanation: Penicillins act on penicillin-binding proteins in the cell wall, not on the ribosome. The targets file describes each page as listing the medicines and drug classes that act on the target, so this reads as penicillins being ribosome inhibitors. Mirror error on targets/penicillin-binding-proteins, whose drugClasses lists 'macrolides'.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove 'penicillins' here (and 'macrolides' on the penicillin-binding-proteins page), or relabel the field as related or contrasting classes.

findings.quote: macrolides
findings.explanation: Macrolides inhibit the 50S ribosomal subunit, not penicillin-binding proteins; the page text itself names beta-lactams as the drugs that bind PBPs. See the mirror error on targets/bacterial-ribosome (drugClasses lists 'penicillins').
findings.suggestedFix: Remove 'macrolides' from drugClasses on this page, or relabel the field as related or contrasting classes.

findings.quote: lung-cancer
findings.explanation: The conditions list includes lung-cancer and colorectal-cancer. Mammography images the breast; it neither detects, stages nor follows either cancer, and the page text never mentions them (looks like a keyword cross-link on 'cancer'). Only breast-cancer fits.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove lung-cancer and colorectal-cancer from conditions.

findings.quote: paracetamol
findings.explanation: Paracetamol does not act at opioid receptors, yet it (and 'non-opioid-analgesics' in drugClasses[1]) is listed against this target, and the targets file describes each page as listing the medicines and classes that act on it. The same pattern recurs elsewhere: ibuprofen and nsaids on xanthine-oxidase (they treat the gout flare, not the enzyme), antiplatelets on factor-xa, metoprolol on beta-2-adrenoceptor (the beta-1 page itself calls it beta-1-selective), prednisolone on insulin-receptor (it acts via the glucocorticoid receptor), paracetamol on cox-2, ACE inhibitors on at1-receptor and ARBs on angiotensin-converting-enzyme. If these are meant as 'related' items they should be labelled so; otherwise readers are told the wrong drug acts on the target.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove or relabel the non-acting drugs and classes across the target pages, starting with those named here.

findings.quote: acl-injury
findings.explanation: ACL tears are assessed clinically and with MRI (the MRI page lists acl-injury); ultrasound has no routine role, and the ultrasound page text only mentions tendon tears and effusions. Same type of cross-link error as the mammography conditions list.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove acl-injury from the ultrasound conditions list.

findings.quote: which shows that the benefit comes from slower downstream changes in receptor sensitivity, gene expression and neural plasticity rather than from the raised serotonin itself
findings.explanation: The delayed onset is an observation; the explanation is a hypothesis, not something it 'shows'. Both the serotonin and the plasticity accounts remain unproven, some benefit can appear within 1-2 weeks, and NHS patient information describes SSRIs as raising serotonin, so 'rather than from the raised serotonin itself' goes beyond the cited sources.
findings.suggestedFix: Soften to 'which suggests that part of the benefit comes from slower downstream changes ... as well as from the raised serotonin'.

findings.quote: which lowers fasting blood glucose without causing hypoglycaemia
findings.explanation: Absolute safety statement. Metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycaemia, but it can contribute when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas (insulin is listed on this very page), with heavy alcohol use or prolonged fasting. The body text is correct ('does not cause low blood sugar on its own'); the summary drops the qualifier.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'rarely causes hypoglycaemia when used alone'.

findings.quote: bleeding from the puncture site that does not stop with pressure, severe pain, spreading redness or swelling, or a limb that turns pale or cold are reasons to contact the care team urgently
findings.explanation: Good that after-care red flags are listed, but two of them are emergencies, not a phone call: bleeding that continues despite firm pressure and a pale, cold limb (arterial occlusion or bleeding at the puncture site). 'Contact the care team' could be read as phoning the ward. UK after-care advice for angiography normally says to press firmly and call 999 or go to A&E.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'seek emergency help (999) for bleeding that does not stop with firm pressure or a pale, cold or numb limb; contact the care team the same day for the other signs'.

findings.quote: cutting acid output by more than 90%
findings.explanation: At standard doses PPIs reduce 24-hour intragastric acidity by roughly 80% (the omeprazole SmPC gives a mean decrease of at least 80% at 20 mg daily, as I recall), approaching 90% only with higher or twice-daily dosing. 'More than 90%' overstates, and the cited NHS and MedlinePlus pages give no figure.
findings.suggestedFix: Use 'most of the acid output (around 80% or more at usual doses)' or drop the number.

findings.quote: the only lifestyle measure that reliably builds bone density
findings.explanation: Overstated. Weight-bearing and resistance exercise are the main lifestyle measures that increase or maintain bone density, but the effect in adults is modest (a few percent), and calcium, vitamin D, protein, not smoking and limiting alcohol also protect bone. Neither the cited WHO fact sheet nor the NHS guidelines page supports 'the only' or 'reliably builds'.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'the main lifestyle measure shown to maintain or modestly increase bone density'.

findings.quote: Anyone who is or might be pregnant unless it is an emergency
findings.explanation: Blanket wording. Chest, limb and dental X-rays deliver a negligible dose to the unborn baby and are done in pregnancy when clinically needed (after telling the radiographer). The page's own risks field is more accurate: 'The abdomen and pelvis are avoided in pregnancy unless the examination is essential'. The blanket line could deter a pregnant woman from a needed chest or limb film.
findings.suggestedFix: Align with the risks field: abdomen and pelvis films are avoided unless essential; other examinations are done when needed after the radiographer is told.

findings.quote: unsaturated fats from olive oil, nuts and oily fish lower LDL cholesterol
findings.explanation: Oily-fish omega-3 fats lower triglycerides but do not lower LDL cholesterol (high-dose DHA can raise it slightly). The LDL benefit comes from replacing saturated fat with olive oil, nuts, seeds and plant oils.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'unsaturated fats from olive oil, nuts and seeds lower LDL when they replace saturated fat; oily fish lowers triglycerides'.

findings.quote: by thickening cervical mucus and thinning the lining (progestogen-only pills and the hormonal coil, which also lightens heavy periods)
findings.explanation: The commonest progestogen-only pill in the UK (desogestrel) works mainly by stopping ovulation (the NHS says so); only older-style progestogen-only pills rely mainly on cervical mucus. The hormonal coil acts mainly locally (mucus, thin lining) and may also suppress ovulation in some users. Grouping every progestogen-only pill under 'mucus and lining' is out of date.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'progestogen-only pills (most stop ovulation, some mainly thicken mucus) and the hormonal coil (mainly thickens mucus and thins the lining)'.

findings.quote: varenicline or cytisine
findings.explanation: UK-first site: to my knowledge cytisine is not a licensed or NHS-commissioned stop-smoking medicine in the UK (NICE NG209 covers nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion and e-cigarettes), although WHO guidance and some other countries use it. Listing it among supports available to UK readers could mislead. I may be out of date as of late 2026.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove cytisine or qualify it ('available in some countries').

findings.quote: they are effective against intracellular organisms such as Chlamydia, Mycoplasma and Legionella that penicillins cannot reach
findings.explanation: Mycoplasma has no cell wall, so beta-lactams are inactive regardless of access, and it lives mainly on the surface of respiratory epithelium rather than inside cells; 'cannot reach' is the wrong reason for it. Chlamydia has almost no peptidoglycan and Legionella is facultatively intracellular.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'atypical organisms such as Chlamydia, Mycoplasma and Legionella, which penicillins do not treat (Mycoplasma has no cell wall; Chlamydia and Legionella live inside cells)'.

notes: Assignment described the third file as treatment targets (blood pressure, glucose, LDL), but content/targets.json holds 24 molecular drug targets (receptors, enzymes, channels, transporters), so there were no clinical target values to compare with NICE, BHF, Diabetes UK or US figures; its numbers are limited to onset times, half-lives and an LDL-lowering range (30 to 55%), which look plausible. Exactly 20 findings, none dropped for the cap. No web access: I could not open any cited page, so statements attributed to NHS, FDA or UKHSA pages (for example UKHSA dose surveys since 1986, about 1,400 lives saved a year, 4 in 100 recalls) were judged from knowledge only and are unverified; findings that depend on a cited page are marked needsSource. The medications and drugClasses lists on target pages look auto-linked and include drugs that do not act on the target (see the mu-opioid-receptor finding), and the conditions lists on imaging pages show a similar problem (mammography, ultrasound): worth a sweep across all such pages. Considered but not reported as too uncertain or minor: imaging/x-ray says a lead apron 'may be placed' (UK guidance since 2020 no longer recommends routine patient shielding); targets/cox-2 says coxibs 'spare the stomach' (they lower, not remove, GI risk); health/exercise says exercise is 'as effective as medication' for mild to moderate depression (low-certainty evidence); health/transgender-health states mental-health disparities are driven 'largely' by rejection and delays rather than by being trans as settled causation, and leans on US guidelines (WPATH, Endocrine Society, UCSF) for monitoring where NHS England protocols differ in places; health/weight links a 15 kg loss to remission in 'about half' (in DiRECT about half of the whole intervention group, about 86% of those losing 15 kg or more).
